# Base Rates and Updating

*Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating*

::: {#chapter-14-start .chapter-epigraph}
> “The great tragedy of Science—the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact.”
>
> — Thomas Henry Huxley, [“Biogenesis and Abiogenesis”](https://aleph0.clarku.edu/huxley/CE8/B-Ab.html), presidential address to the British Association, 1870
:::

A candidate passes a screening test that is described as “80 percent accurate.” The committee wants to use the result to reduce hiring mistakes. How confident should it now be that the candidate will meet the performance standard? The number sounds decisive, but it does not yet answer the question. Eighty percent of *what*? How common are strong performers in the applicant pool? How often does the screen pass a weaker candidate? Was the test validated on a comparable population and outcome?

The committee needs to know how many applicants who pass will perform well. The report may instead say how many strong performers pass. One starts with everyone who passed; the other starts with everyone who meets the performance standard. Confusing the two groups could turn an informative screen into unjustified confidence about whom to hire. We will begin by counting them separately, then use that distinction to interpret the evidence. The optional mathematical analyses express the same reasoning in notation.

::: {.callout-note .core-idea icon=false}
## Core Idea

A positive screen can come from someone who meets the standard or someone who does not. To interpret the result, count both routes in the relevant population. Bayes' rule organizes this comparison, while its usefulness depends on the evidence and assumptions supplied to it.

:::

## Learning goals

- Use complement, intersection, union, and conditional probability without changing the event or denominator.
- Translate a Bayesian update into natural frequencies and select defensible reference classes.
- Diagnose base-rate neglect, reversed conditionals, conjunction errors, and information dilution.


## Worked update: the same screen in two applicant pools

A validated screen may look like a portable measure of candidate quality. Yet the same positive result can mean different things in different applicant pools. To see why, return to the hiring screen.

Suppose that 20% of applicants in a broad pool would meet a clearly defined performance standard, the screen passes 80% of those future strong performers, and it also passes 30% of the others. Among 10,000 applicants:

- 2,000 would meet the standard; 1,600 pass the screen.
- 8,000 would not; 2,400 nevertheless pass.
- Of 4,000 positive screens, 1,600 are true positives.

Under those assumptions, 1,600 of the 4,000 applicants who pass would perform strongly: 40%. The screen can be meaningfully informative—it raises the probability from 20% to 40%—without making a positive result decisive.

Now place the same screen in a carefully preselected pool where 50% would meet the standard. Assume its **sensitivity**, the share of strong performers who pass, and its **false-positive rate**, the share of others who pass, remain unchanged. Among 10,000 applicants it produces 4,000 true positives and 1,500 false positives, so the probability of strong performance after a positive screen is about 72.7%. Interpreting a sensitivity figure requires the starting population and evidence that the test performs similarly in it.

## Probability begins with a model

The hiring calculation became useful only after the applicants and possible results were organized into a common population. Without that structure, a percentage can answer a different question from the one the decision requires.

A **sample space** lists the elementary outcomes allowed by a model. An **event** collects the outcomes of interest, such as finishing a project by Friday. Probabilities range from zero to one, and the probability of some outcome in the complete sample space is one. Probabilities add when events are mutually exclusive. Calling a coin fair, successive observations independent, or an applicant pool comparable to the validation sample are substantive assumptions.

[]{#complement-preserve-the-event-boundary}

An event and its **complement** cover all possibilities without overlapping. If a project has a 70% probability of finishing by Friday, the remaining 30% is the probability of not finishing by Friday under the same model. “Not finished by Friday” is not the same event as “the project fails.” A complement works only when the time horizon and outcome definition remain fixed.

[]{#and-use-the-conditional-branch}

To find the probability that two events both occur, start with the chance of the first and multiply by the chance of the second *among cases where the first occurs*. If the events are independent, learning that the first occurred does not change the chance of the second.

Independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity. Rain and traffic delay can occur together and may be dependent. Two cards drawn without replacement are dependent because the first draw changes the deck.

[]{#or-restore-the-overlap}

To find the probability that at least one of two events occurs, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap. That last step prevents double counting.

A project can be delayed by a supplier problem, a software problem, or both. Adding the separate probabilities as though the routes were disjoint exaggerates total risk; considering only the most vivid route understates it.

## Conditional direction matters

A **conditional probability** concerns a specified group of cases. In the hiring example, asking what share of strong performers pass starts with the strong performers. The committee instead needs the share of those who pass who are strong performers. Changing the starting group changes the question.

The same reversal appears in court. A one-in-a-million probability of a DNA profile among unrelated people is not a one-in-a-million probability that a matched defendant is innocent. The latter depends on how the suspect was selected, how many people were compared, laboratory error, relatedness, the prior probability of different sources, and the rest of the case (Thompson & Schumann, 1987).

Conditional probability also makes independence explicit. Events are independent when learning one does not change the probability of the other. Zero correlation is not generally equivalent to independence: it rules out one linear relationship, not every probabilistic dependence.

:::: {#math-probability-rules}
::: {.callout-note .research-lens .mathematical-analysis icon=false collapse=true}
## Mathematical analysis: probability rules and their notation

Let $\Omega$ be the sample space, $A$ and $B$ events, and $A^c$ the complement of $A$. The basic rules are

$$
0\le P(A)\le 1, \qquad P(\Omega)=1,
$$

with additivity for mutually exclusive events. Complement, intersection (AND), and union (OR) are written as

$$
P(A^c)=1-P(A),
$$

$$
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A),
$$

$$
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
$$

Provided $P(B)>0$, conditional probability is

$$
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
$$

Everything after the vertical bar identifies the group being counted within. Thus $P(\text{positive screen}\mid\text{strong performance})$ and $P(\text{strong performance}\mid\text{positive screen})$ answer different questions. For independent events, $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$ when the conditional is defined.
:::
::::

## Bayes' rule restores the alternatives

A positive result supports an explanation when it is more expected under that explanation than under its alternatives. Counting only the cases where the explanation is true leaves out the competing route to the same evidence. Bayes’ rule brings both routes into the comparison.

The **prior** gives the starting probability, which is the prevalence of strong performance in this screening example. The **likelihood** asks how probable the evidence would be if the explanation held. The competing likelihood asks how often the same evidence appears without that explanation. The **posterior** is the probability after incorporating the evidence (Bayes, 1763).

To update, count the cases where the explanation produces the evidence, then compare them with *all* cases that could produce it. For the hiring screen, both strong and weaker performers can pass.

:::: {#math-bayes-rule}
::: {.callout-note .research-lens .mathematical-analysis icon=false collapse=true}
## Mathematical analysis: Bayes' rule

If $A$ and $A^c$ partition the cases, total probability rebuilds the denominator:

$$
P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c).
$$

Bayes' rule then reverses the conditioning without reversing the evidence:

$$
P(A\mid B)=
\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}
{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)}.
$$

Here $P(A)$ is the prior, $P(B\mid A)$ is the likelihood under the explanation, and $P(B\mid A^c)$ is the likelihood under its alternative. The posterior is $P(A\mid B)$. In the hiring example, this gives $1{,}600/4{,}000=0.40$.
:::
::::

For the committee, the update is useful only if these inputs describe the applicants and performance standard it actually faces. Selection into the pool, changes in working conditions, and uncertainty about the test’s error rates all affect that judgment.


## Natural frequencies make Bayes visible

Translating percentages into people makes it easier to inspect who could have produced a positive result.

For a second hypothetical example, suppose 1 percent of a population has a disease. A test is positive for 90 percent of people who have it and for 9 percent of people who do not. A person tests positive. The tempting answer is 90 percent, but that describes how often people with the disease test positive. We need to know how often people with a positive test have the disease.

Imagine 10,000 people:

- 100 have the disease; 90 test positive.
- 9,900 do not; 891 test positive.
- Of 981 positive tests, 90 are true positives.

Of the 981 people who test positive, 90 have the disease: about 9.17%.

![A positive result can come from either group. In this hypothetical population, the much larger group without disease supplies most of the positive tests.](../figures/probability-judgment-map.svg){#fig-probability-judgment-map fig-alt="A natural-frequency tree starts with 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and 9,900 do not. With ninety-percent sensitivity, 90 people with disease test positive. With a nine-percent false-positive rate, 891 people without disease test positive. Therefore 90 of the 981 positive tests, about 9.2 percent, come from people with disease." width=100%}

The two branches in @fig-probability-judgment-map answer the crucial question: who could have produced this positive result? Natural frequencies preserve those nested sets, often making Bayesian reasoning more transparent than isolated percentages (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). They expose the denominator that the 90% sensitivity figure leaves implicit.

## Reference classes are judgment calls

The calculation asks for a base rate, but the decision rarely supplies an uncontested comparison group. Should a start-up be compared with all new firms, firms in the same sector, firms at the same funding stage, or firms with similarly experienced founders? A narrow class may be more relevant but noisier. A broad class is more stable but less tailored. Choosing the class is therefore part of the substantive judgment, and it can change the recommendation even when the arithmetic is correct.

Base-rate neglect is more likely when individuating detail feels causal and the statistic feels incidental (Bar-Hillel, 1980). The outside view therefore begins with comparable cases before explaining why the focal case differs (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993). A defensible analysis reports several nested classes, shows whether the conclusion changes, and identifies which differences are genuinely diagnostic. [Chapter 15](15-samples-randomness-regression-and-calibration.qmd#small-samples-swing-widely) examines the sampling uncertainty that remains even after the class is well chosen.

Return to hiring. The base rate should concern future performance under the organization's role, support, and criterion—not an undefined pool of “talent.” The screen's sensitivity and false-positive rate must come from a comparable applicant population. If the criterion rewards manager similarity rather than job output, the posterior can be mathematically correct and substantively wrong.

[]{#research-lens-conjunction-disjunction-and-dilution}

::: {.callout-note .research-lens icon=false}
## Research Lens: conjunction, disjunction, and dilution

[Chapter 9](09-what-feels-likely-availability-affect-and-resemblance.qmd#when-category-fit-substitutes-for-probability-resemblance) showed why a coherent story can feel probable. The set relation is straightforward: requiring two conditions cannot make an event more probable than requiring just one, while allowing either of two routes cannot make it less probable than either route alone.

Adding a condition makes the event a subset. “A bank teller active in a social movement” cannot be more probable than “a bank teller,” however well the detail matches the description (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). By contrast, adding alternative routes expands a union. The probability that a project is delayed by *at least one* of several causes cannot be smaller than the probability of any single route, though overlaps must be handled rather than simply added.

More detail is not always more information. Weakly diagnostic detail can dilute attention to stronger evidence. Sivanathan and Kakkar (2017) found that adding minor side effects to serious drug side effects could reduce perceived overall severity. Group evidence by severity, probability, and decision relevance so completeness does not destroy structure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Check your denominator

For each prompt, write the target conditional before answering.

1. Seventy percent of successful trainees used a practice platform. What additional quantities are needed to estimate the probability of success among platform users?
2. Ten percent of projects suffer supplier delay and 12% suffer software delay. What must be known before adding the percentages?
3. A screen validated in experienced applicants is applied to entry-level applicants. Which part of the Bayesian model may no longer transport?


:::


## Practice Lab

Take one positive test, screening result, warning signal, or performance indicator. Produce a one-page **Bayesian audit** using a population of 10,000. State the target conditional probability, choose and defend two plausible reference classes, show true positives and false positives under each, and identify one omitted alternative or measurement problem. The observable output is the two natural-frequency trees and a decision rule that states what action changes at which posterior range.

## Take it forward

The committee can now replace “the screen is 80 percent accurate” with a meaningful account: who was screened, how often each kind of applicant passed, and what a positive result implies in this pool. Before using a striking percentage, identify its denominator and the alternative route by which the same evidence could appear.
